Hi All, 

I appreciate any help I can get.  Just let me know if this isn't the right forum.  First I tried to use ezPredict on my data, but that didn't work so I tried an example from the documentation.  That worked, so I tried altering the lmer object by adding one continuous variable but  ezPredict didn't like that.  Code and error below.  

data(ANT)
ANT$nor <- rnorm(nrow(ANT), 0,1)
head(ANT)

#fit a mixed effects model to the rt data
rt_fit = lmer(
  formula = rt ~ cue*flank*group + nor + (1|subnum)
  , data = ANT[ANT$error==0,]
)
#obtain the predictions from the model
rt_preds = ezPredict(
  fit = rt_fit
)

My sincere apologies for failing to reply earlier. 

The problem with your example is that ezPredict wants to obtain predictions for every combination of every level of every predictor in the model, which can blow up when you have a continuous predictor in the mix with lots of levels. To constain things, set the value of the "numeric_res" argument to something like 10:

rt_preds = ezPredict(
        fit = rt_fit

, numeric_res = 10
    )

messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] starting at the beginning
parts:
Hm, I can't seem to reproduce the error you mentioned. What is the output when you do str(rt_preds)?

Regarding the influence on inference of limiting the numeric resolution of the obtained predictions: 

It'll only matter if you're using ezPredict's output to compute something like the region of the continuous predictor over which the model suggests that some difference manifests (either the mean is different from zero, or the difference between two groups is different from zero). When doing this, you'll want to use a numeric_res that matches your desired precision of inference. One approach is to start with a low precision then use the "to_predict" argument to construct more focused higher resolution predictions of the areas of interest. 

Otherwise, if you're simply using ezPredict/ezPlot2 to visualize the nature of the continuous effect, if you're using a linear model then you really only need predictions at the endpoints to characterize the slope, though you'll probably also want some decent coverage through the middle to show how the CI gets tighter in the center of the data. If you're using a potentially-non-linear gam and want to visualize the nature of the potentially-non-linear effect, use at a minimum as many points as the gam derived estimated degrees of freedom (excluding degrees contributed by random effects), maybe twice that to ensure you're capturing the possibly uneven distribution of knots.

Is there a way to plot multiple predictions on the same graph and use color/line-style to differentiate them?

Yup:

    preds1 = ezPredict(...)
    preds2 = ezPredict(...)
    preds_both = list(
        cells = rbind(
            cbind(
                preds1$cells
                , version = '1'
            )
            , cbind(
                preds2$cells
                , version = '2'
            )
        )
        boots = rbind(
            cbind(
                preds1$boots
                , version = '1'
            )
            , cbind(
                preds2$boots
                , version = '2'
            )
        )
    )
    ezPlot2(
        preds = preds_both
        , x = ...
        , split = version
    )
